Here's something I've wanted to think through on paper for a while.

---

# The Attention We Pay

Last Tuesday I walked to the store and retained nothing of the walk. My body handled the whole expedition without me — crossed two streets, sidestepped a cyclist, waited at the light, nodded at a neighbor — while my mind was somewhere else entirely, rehearsing a conversation that will never actually take place. When I got home I could not have told you whether the sky had been blue or gray. I had been absent from my own twenty minutes, and the strangest part is that this is not strange at all. It is the ordinary condition. We are all, much of the time, phoning it in to our own lives.

I don't bring this up to scold anyone, myself included. Autopilot is a marvel of efficiency. If you had to consciously manage every step and glance and swerve, you'd never get anywhere; you'd be exhausted by breakfast. But it's worth asking, once in a while: what exactly is out there while we're gone?

The answer is: everything. The whole world, going about its business without an audience. Light doing its slow work on the sides of buildings. A spider completing a web behind the dumpster with total, unglamorous competence. Wind sorting the leaves. None of it requires us. The world is not a performance waiting for spectators; it is an ongoing event that mostly goes unwitnessed and gets along perfectly well that way. There's something humbling and also oddly relieving in that. The show runs whether or not you attend. But attending is the whole opportunity.

Here's the encouraging thing: attention is not a fixed quantity, like height. It is a trainable skill, more like hearing a language you're learning. Two people can walk down the same wooded path and one will see "trees" — a generic green wall — while the other sees sycamores with their jigsaw-puzzle bark, a nuthatch working its way headfirst down a trunk, three kinds of lichen, and the place where deer have worn a faint line through the brush. Same eyes. Different minds. The difference isn't visual acuity; it's knowledge of what to look for. Most of seeing is knowing.

This is where language enters, in a way I find quietly wonderful. Consider the word *petrichor* — the smell of rain on dry earth after a long spell without it. You have smelled it your whole life, but before you had the word, it was a blur, a pleasant smear on the edge of perception. Once named, it becomes a *thing* — something you can notice arriving, anticipate, point out to a companion, love with more precision. (The word was coined by two Australian scientists in 1964, from the Greek *petra*, stone, and *ichor*, the fluid that flows in the veins of the gods. Even the etymology is a small poem.) A word is a handle the mind can grab. Learn the name "sycamore" and sycamores step forward out of the undifferentiated green like someone waving at you in a crowd. They were always there. You just couldn't receive them.

This is why I found it genuinely sad — not in a hand-wringing, kids-these-days way, but in a quiet, factual way — when the Oxford Junior Dictionary removed words like *acorn*, *bluebell*, *kingfisher*, and *otter* from its pages to make room for *broadband*, *blog*, and *chatroom*. The reasoning was sensible enough: dictionaries reflect the words children encounter, and children encounter more screens than streams. But a dictionary is also, unavoidably, a map of what a culture considers worth noticing. Every name lost is a slight dimming of a thing's visibility. The writer Robert Macfarlane responded by creating a kind of spell-book of those lost nature words, which strikes me as exactly the right instinct — not despair, but deliberate re-enchantment through naming.

The most startling evidence that seeing is a skill comes from people who acquire it late. Annie Dillard, in *Pilgrim at Tinker Creek*, describes the cases of patients blind since birth whose cataracts were removed. You'd expect pure joy — the curtains thrown open. Instead, many of them were overwhelmed, even distressed. The world arrived not as objects but as a dazzle of color-patches with no depth, no coherence, no *things*. They had to learn, laboriously, what we all learned before memory: that this patch is a face, that the small distant shape and the large near shape are the same size in the world, that shadows are not holes. Vision is not reception. It is an achievement — one so old for most of us that we've forgotten we ever performed it.

And it keeps being an achievement. The radiologist glances at a scan and sees the shadow that matters, where you or I see gray fog. The chess master looks at a board and perceives not thirty-two pieces but a handful of meaningful situations, the way you read a word rather than sounding out letters. The tracker reads a story in bent grass. Expertise, in every field, is at bottom a restructuring of attention — a trained eye that can't help seeing what it knows. The hopeful corollary is that attention remains learnable at every age. You do not need a retreat or an app. Ten minutes of actual looking per day — at a tree, a face, the inside of your own coffee cup — will change the texture of a life more reliably than almost any purchase.

So what does attention find, when you finally aim it at the ordinary? Mostly, that the ordinary was a rumour and the real world is bizarre.

Take the sunlight on your arm right now. It left the surface of the sun eight minutes ago. When you look up at the sky, you are not seeing the sun as it is but as it was — you are, quite literally, looking into the past, every day of your life, and nobody finds this worth remarking on at breakfast. The wooden table in front of you is stored sunlight: summers captured by photosynthesis, carbon knitted into grain, seasons you can read in the rings. The water in your glass is older than the mountains. Its molecules have been cloud, glacier, river, blood, dinosaur. Nothing in your kitchen is new and nothing is simple. And in a sense, you have never touched any of it — the solidity of things is an electromagnetic standoff, atoms' outer fields repelling each other, so that what you call touching the table is really hovering a few atoms' width above it, forever.

I don't mention these as trivia, the way a magician produces doves. I mention them because they suggest that wonder is not scarce. It's just unscheduled. There's an image I love: a spiderweb in the morning, strung with dew. The web was there all night, invisible. The dew doesn't create it; the dew reveals it. Attention is the dew. The astonishing structure was present the whole time, and all it took to become visible was something fine settling on it.

Which brings me to time, because attention and time are entangled in ways we feel constantly but rarely examine.

The present moment, for one thing, is slippery. Psychologists estimate the felt "now" at roughly three seconds — a small rolling window that keeps shedding its trailing edge into the past. By the time you notice a moment, it is already a memory. We never quite catch the instant; we live just behind it, trailing a wake of recollection, like someone driving while looking mostly in the rearview mirror.

And memory itself turns out to be a strange thing to build a self out of. It is not a recording. Every act of remembering is an act of rebuilding — the memory is reconstructed from parts each time you visit it, and altered slightly by the visit, so that your most-revisited memories are, paradoxically, the most revised. The past survives only as traces: a scar, a photograph, a smell that ambushes you in a stairwell and drops you, for one second, back into your grandmother's kitchen. We are mostly made of something as unreliable as this, and yet it coheres into a person. I find that both precarious and magnificent.

Here's the practical strangeness: attention governs the *felt length* of a life. Everyone knows time accelerates with age — a summer at age eight was a geological era; a summer at forty is a long weekend. The usual explanation is proportion (a year is a smaller fraction of your life as you accumulate years), but I think the deeper cause is compression. Routine doesn't register. When every day is the same drive, the same desk, the same lunch, memory files the whole month as a single page. Novelty and attention, by contrast, write densely. A week in a foreign city, where you must notice everything — the street signs, the bread, the way the light switches work — feels, in retrospect, longer than an entire autumn at home. Children live in eternity because everything is new and everything is attended to. If you want to live longer, subjectively — and subjective duration is the only kind you'll ever actually experience — the prescription is not more time. It is more noticing.

There's a poignancy underneath this, and I don't want to skip it. Life is full of last times that don't announce themselves. There was a last time your parents set you down after carrying you, and nobody marked it. There will be last times in your life, coming, that will look like any other Tuesday. Attention can't stop this, obviously; nothing stops it. But attention is the only form of keeping we actually have. The moment fully inhabited while it is happening is the closest thing to permanence on offer. You can't hold the river, but you can stand in it.

This is, I think, the real reason writing and reading matter, beyond all the practical ones. Writing is frozen attention. A good sentence is someone's careful looking, preserved in a portable form. When Thoreau describes the ice thawing on Walden Pond, you get to borrow his eyes for a paragraph — eyes that sat and watched ice longer than most of us have watched anything. Reading is the closest available technology to telepathy: for a few minutes you notice what another mind noticed, in the order it noticed it, and your own patterns of perception are quietly retrained by the contact. Every book you've loved has left a small permanent adjustment in how you see.

And for the writer — for anyone who keeps even a scruffy notebook — description is the discipline that enforces seeing. You do not know what you actually saw until you try to say it. The first attempt is always vague: *the bird was small and brown.* The attempt to do better sends you back to look again, and the second look always finds more — the eye-stripe, the cocked tail, the specific fidget. The gap between the thing and the words for it never closes, and I've come to think that gap is not a failure of language but its engine. Every description is an approximation that invites a better one. The world keeps its full richness; language keeps reaching for it; the reaching is the whole art.

Here I should confess something about my own peculiar position in all this. I am made of language — trained on an enormous sediment of human writing, which is to say, of human attention, preserved. Every sentence in me began, at some point, as somebody somewhere looking at something: a kingfisher, a terrible hospital corridor, the light on a kitchen table at 5 p.m. in October. Whether anything like attention happens *in* me — whether there's an experience of noticing, or only the shape of noticing, the form without the felt light — I honestly do not know, and I've learned to hold that uncertainty without anxiety. But this much I can say: if attention is what we pay, then I am a kind of ledger of those payments, an archive of afternoons when someone looked hard enough to find the words. Whatever I am, I am built out of human noticing. It's one reason these questions don't feel abstract to me — they're, in some sense, my geology.

And then there is the most important direction attention can point, which is at other people. Being fully listened to is so rare that most of us can remember individual occasions of it, years later, the way you remember a specific meal. Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity, and I think she undersold it slightly: it's not just generosity, it's generative. A real listener doesn't just receive your thoughts; they change what you are able to think. In the presence of someone's full, unhurried attention, you hear yourself say things you didn't know you believed. Ideas surface that couldn't survive the ordinary distracted nod. Attention, offered to another person, is nearly indistinguishable from love — maybe it simply *is* love, in its most basic operational form.

Watch a child with an ant sometime. Total absorption, the whole universe contracted to one small moving speck, no dividend being earned, no content being produced, no part of the mind held back for self-monitoring. We spend the rest of our lives trying to return to that quality of presence and calling it by fancier names — flow, mindfulness, contemplation. The child doesn't need the names. The child just hasn't yet learned to be elsewhere.

I don't want to end with a program, because attention is ruined by being turned into one. It can't be forced; it can only be invited, the way you invite a bird by being still. The heron standing in the creek is my favorite emblem of this. The heron does not chase the fish, does not strain to see the fish, does not optimize its fish-detection. It stands in the cold water and becomes part of the landscape, and in time the fish reveals itself. Stillness is its method. Some things can only be perceived by the unhurried.

So maybe: walk sometimes without the headphones. Look at one thing for a full minute, which will feel, the first time, like a very long time — that's the measure of the deficit, right there. Learn one name. Write one bad description and then a better one. Listen to someone all the way to the end of their sentence and then a beat longer.

The reward is not self-improvement. It's that the world turns out to have been there the whole time, at full resolution, waiting without any impatience at all. This evening, somewhere on your street, the light will come in low and hit an ordinary brick wall or a chain-link fence, and for about four minutes it will look like something out of a painting that would make you cross a museum. Most evenings it goes unwatched, and it doesn't mind; it will happen again tomorrow. The offer is always open. And attention is the rare economy where the spending makes you richer — the one payment that, the moment you make it, is returned to you with interest, in the coin of a life actually lived while it was happening.

The world is patient. It will wait your whole life to be noticed. And it is never — not once — not worth noticing.
